pos: n. (ruin, undoing; rendering Hebrew shachath and abaddon, Greek apoleia)
etymology: From the Latin destructio, from destruo, to pull down. Hebrew abaddon is from abad, to perish, and is used as a name for the place of the dead; Greek apoleia is from apollumi, to destroy utterly — the same root gives Apollyon, the destroyer, in Revelation 9.
biblical_def: Destruction is ruin, and Scripture insists it is a destination rather than an accident. Proverbs supplies the best-known diagnosis of how men arrive there: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18) — the sequence is stated as a law, and the fall is the visible part of a collapse that began invisibly in the heart. The Psalter uses the word of mortality under God's hand: “Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men” (Psalm 90:3), where death is not a natural wearing out but a divine word spoken over the race. Paul defines the final sense precisely, and the definition is essential: the disobedient “shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). Everlasting destruction is not a phrase annihilation can hold — a destruction that is over is not everlasting — and the words that follow define it as banishment from the presence of the Lord. Romans traces it to God's sovereign patience: he “endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction” (Romans 9:22), so that even the destroyed are the objects of a longsuffering they despised.
webster_summary: Ruin, undoing. Scripture makes it a destination reached by a road — pride goeth before destruction — and defines the final form as everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.
webster_full: DESTRUCTION, n. [L. destructio, from destruo, to pull down.] The act of destroying; demolition; a pulling down; subversion; ruin.
2. The state of being destroyed; as, a city given to destruction.
3. Death; murder; slaughter; massacre.
4. Cause of destruction; a consuming plague; a destroyer.
5. In Scripture, eternal death; as, everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, 2 Thess. 1.
corruption_summary: Destruction is read as extinction, and the word is enlisted to prove annihilationism. Paul calls it everlasting and defines it as exclusion from the presence of the Lord, which is a state endured rather than an event concluded.
corruption_paragraphs: The annihilationist argument leans on the ordinary meaning of destroy: what is destroyed ceases to exist. But Scripture uses the word for ruin rather than for cessation of being. A ruined garment or a broken vessel still exists; it has been undone with respect to what it was for. 2 Thessalonians 1:9 settles the question by attaching two modifiers that annihilation cannot carry — the destruction is everlasting, and it consists in being from the presence of the Lord. A thing that no longer exists is not away from anything, and a completed extinction is not everlasting; it is instantaneous and then finished.

The principle to recover is that Scripture presents this ruin as the end of a road men walk, not a fate imposed at random. Proverbs 16:18 names pride as the first step, and Romans 9:22 says the vessels of wrath were endured with much longsuffering. Both texts remove any charge of arbitrariness: God is patient with those who are heading there, and the pride that leads them is their own. That is precisely why the warning is preached — while the longsuffering lasts, the road can still be left.
roots_summary: Hebrew shachath is a pit or corruption, from a root meaning to go to ruin, and abaddon is the place of destruction. Greek apoleia is utter loss or ruin, from apollumi, to destroy.
roots_lines: Hebrew shachath (H7845) — a pit, corruption, destruction; thou wilt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.
Hebrew abaddon (H11) — destruction, the place of the dead; from abad, to perish.
Hebrew sheber (H7667) — a breaking, a fracture, ruin; the destruction of the daughter of my people.
Greek apoleia (G684) — utter ruin, perdition; the broad way leadeth to it.
Greek olethros (G3639) — ruin, destruction; the word in everlasting destruction, 2 Thessalonians 1:9.

Of mortality under God's word: thou turnest man to destruction (Psalm 90:3).
Of the final state defined: everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9).

pos: n. (force used to injure; rendering Hebrew chamas, Greek bia)
etymology: From the Latin violentia, from vis, force. Hebrew chamas is the word Genesis uses of the pre-flood world, and it covers wrong done by force generally — not only bloodshed but oppression, extortion, and the perversion of justice; it is violence as the ruin of right order.
biblical_def: Violence is the reason given for the Flood, which makes it the sin Scripture first names as calling down universal judgment: “The earth also was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence” (Genesis 6:11). The Hebrew chamas is broader than bloodshed — it takes in the oppression of the weak and the bending of justice — and it is repeated twice more in the following verses, as though the narrator cannot say it enough. The Psalter records God's settled attitude in terms that leave no room for admiration of force: “the wicked and him that loveth violence his soul hateth” (Psalm 11:5). Habakkuk shows the righteous man's response, which is to complain to God about it: “O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!” (Habakkuk 1:2) — a prayer Scripture preserves without rebuke, and the whole book is God's answer to it. Most importantly, violence is what the Servant did not do and what was done to him: “he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither was any deceit in his mouth” (Isaiah 53:9).
webster_summary: Force used to injure — in Hebrew chamas, wrong done by force, including oppression and perverted justice. It filled the earth before the Flood; God's soul hates him that loveth it; and the Servant had done none.
webster_full: VIOLENCE, n. [L. violentia, from vis, force.] Physical force; strength of action or motion applied to injure.
2. Outrage; unjust force; injury done to person or property.
3. Vehemence; impetuosity; as, the violence of passion.
4. Infringement; assault upon what is sacred; as, violence done to a covenant.
5. In Scripture, the earth was filled with violence, Gen. 6; he had done no violence, Isa. 53.
corruption_summary: Violence is treated as a policy failure to be engineered away, or else glamorised as strength. Scripture traces it to the human heart, names it the cause of the Flood, and says God hates the man who loves it.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic and political accounts of violence locate it in conditions — poverty, inequality, upbringing — and conclude that adjusting the conditions will remove it. Scripture grants that conditions matter and denies that they are the source. Genesis 6:5 gives the diagnosis immediately before naming the violence: every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually. Our Lord says the same, that out of the heart proceed murders. A civilisation that never asks about the heart will keep being surprised by its own violence.

The opposite distortion admires force, and it appears in the church whenever strength is confused with the willingness to dominate. Psalm 11:5 forbids it in the strongest possible language: God's soul hates the one who loves violence. The principle to recover is Isaiah 53:9, which sets the pattern of Christian power. The one man with the right and the ability to destroy his enemies did no violence, and was numbered with transgressors; and Peter draws the conclusion for believers under injustice — when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamas is violence, wrong, oppression — injustice by force. Greek bia is force and biastes a violent man; harpage is plundering or extortion.
roots_lines: Hebrew chamas (H2555) — violence, wrong, cruelty; the sin that filled the earth before the Flood.

Greek bia (G970) — force, violence; used of the mob at Ephesus and of the sea's violence.
Greek harpage (G724) — plundering, extortion; within they are full of extortion and excess.

pos: n. (killing, especially of animals or in great numbers; rendering Hebrew tebach, Greek sphage)
etymology: From the Saxon slaht, from slean, to slay — the same root as slay and slew. Hebrew tebach is a butchering, the killing of an animal for food or sacrifice, so the word carries the atmosphere of the shambles rather than of the battlefield.
biblical_def: Slaughter is butchering, and Scripture's central use of it is the silence of the Servant: “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7). It is the passage the Ethiopian eunuch was reading when Philip joined his chariot, and it is the plainest Old Testament statement that the Messiah would be killed as a sacrificial animal is killed — without resistance and without protest. Proverbs uses the same figure for the young man walking into sin without any idea what is happening to him: “He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks” (Proverbs 7:22) — the beast walks calmly because it does not know the destination. Jeremiah asks God to deal with the prosperous wicked in these terms: “pull them out like sheep for the slaughter, and prepare them for the day of slaughter” (Jeremiah 12:3). And Paul quotes the Psalter to describe the church's ordinary condition: “we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter” (Romans 8:36) — immediately before saying we are more than conquerors.
webster_summary: Butchering; killing as of animals. Scripture's chief use is Isaiah 53:7, the Servant brought as a lamb to the slaughter and opening not his mouth — and the church accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
webster_full: SLAUGHTER, n. slaw'ter. [Sax. slaht, from slean, to slay.] A killing; destruction of life by violence.
2. The killing of oxen or other beasts for market; butchery.
3. Great destruction of life by violence; carnage; as, a great slaughter in battle.
4. In Scripture, of the Servant; as, he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, Isa. 53.
5. Of the church's affliction; as, we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter, Rom. 8.
corruption_summary: The cross is recast as tragedy, miscarriage of justice, or moral demonstration. Isaiah's image is a sacrificial animal led to the block — deliberate, appointed, and silently accepted.
corruption_paragraphs: Every attempt to make the crucifixion something other than a sacrifice must get past Isaiah 53:7, and past Philip's use of it. The eunuch asked whether the prophet spoke of himself or of some other man, and Philip began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus. The imagery is not of a hero cut down or of a martyr making a point; it is of a lamb going to the block. The silence matters too: he opened not his mouth. He was not overpowered, and he did not protest, because the death was the errand.

The principle to recover is what Romans 8:36 does with the same figure. Paul applies the slaughter language to the church — killed all the day long, accounted as sheep for the slaughter — and then, without changing the subject, says that in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us. Christian victory is not the avoidance of the slaughter but conquest through it, on the pattern of the Lamb. Proverbs 7:22 supplies the sober warning about a different procession: the man walking into sin is also going to a slaughter, and calmly, because he cannot see the end of the road.
roots_summary: Hebrew tebach is a butchering or slaughter, from tabach, to slay an animal. Greek sphage is slaughter, from sphazo, the verb used of the Lamb slain in Revelation.

pos: n. (a deadly epidemic; rendering Hebrew deber, Greek loimos)
etymology: From the Latin pestilentia, from pestis, a plague. Hebrew deber is a plague or murrain, and it stands in the prophets as one of a standing set of covenant judgments — sword, famine, pestilence, and the noisome beast — announced together as God's four sore judgments.
biblical_def: Pestilence is deadly epidemic disease, and Scripture treats it as one of God's instruments rather than as an event outside his government. Ezekiel names the standing set: “my four sore judgments upon Jerusalem, the sword, and the famine, and the noisome beast, and the pestilence, to cut off from it man and beast” (Ezekiel 14:21). It falls after David's sin in numbering the people, and the narrative is careful to attribute it directly: “So the LORD sent a pestilence upon Israel from the morning even to the time appointed” (2 Samuel 24:15) — and equally careful to record that it stopped at a threshingfloor where an altar was built and sacrifice offered. Jeremiah announces it as the answer to a people whose religion had become formality: “when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them: but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence” (Jeremiah 14:12). Yet the Psalter promises the believer God's protection in exactly the same vocabulary: “Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence” (Psalm 91:3). Both are true, and both are God's doing.
webster_summary: A deadly epidemic. Scripture lists it among God's four sore judgments with sword, famine, and beast — and in the same vocabulary promises deliverance from the noisome pestilence.
webster_full: PESTILENCE, n. [L. pestilentia, from pestis, plague.] Plague; an infectious or contagious disease of a malignant and destructive kind.
2. Corruption; moral disease destructive to happiness; as, the pestilence of error.
3. Anything that is noxious to morals or to the peace of society.
4. In Scripture, one of the four sore judgments; as, the sword, the famine, the noisome beast, and the pestilence, Ezek. 14.
5. Of deliverance; as, he shall deliver thee from the noisome pestilence, Psa. 91.
corruption_summary: Epidemic disease is either explained wholly by second causes with no Governor above them, or else read as a targeted verdict on the individuals it reaches. Scripture affirms God's hand and forbids the confident private verdict.
corruption_paragraphs: The naturalist frame is not wrong about mechanisms — contagion has causes, and Scripture itself legislated quarantine in Leviticus 13 long before germ theory. The error is treating a full account of second causes as a complete account. Amos asks whether there is evil in a city and the LORD hath not done it, and 2 Samuel 24:15 says plainly that the LORD sent the pestilence. Providence is not confined to what medicine cannot explain.

The opposite error reads a plague as a scoreboard and assigns guilt to the dead. Our Lord forbids exactly this reasoning about those on whom the tower in Siloam fell: think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. The principle to recover is that a judgment in the earth is a summons to everyone who hears of it rather than a verdict on those it struck. And Psalm 91:3 keeps the believer's confidence where it belongs: not in immunity, but in a God who delivers, and who did not spare his own Son.
roots_summary: Hebrew deber is pestilence or murrain, and maggephah is a plague or stroke. Greek loimos is a pestilence, listed by our Lord among the signs preceding the end.

pos: n. (a trap for birds or beasts; rendering Hebrew pach and moqesh, Greek pagis)
etymology: From the Saxon snear, a cord. Hebrew pach is the fowler's net or snare, and moqesh is the bait-stick of a trap — the part that looks harmless and springs the mechanism — which is exactly the picture Scripture wants when it speaks of temptation.
biblical_def: Snare is a hidden trap, and every biblical use turns on concealment: a snare that could be seen would catch nothing. The Psalter promises deliverance from it as the first of God's protections: “Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence” (Psalm 91:3), and celebrates escape in the language of a bird that got free: “Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped” (Psalm 124:7) — note that the deliverance came by the breaking of the snare, not by the bird's strength. Proverbs identifies the commonest snare in a single line: “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe” (Proverbs 29:25), which sets the two fears against each other and makes the fear of the LORD the antidote to the fear of men. Paul warns that office in the church has its own particular danger and requires a man's reputation outside the church as a safeguard: an overseer “must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil” (1 Timothy 3:7).
webster_summary: A hidden trap, so called because it cannot be seen. Scripture's commonest snare is the fear of man; the deliverance in Psalm 124 comes by the snare being broken, not by the bird's own strength.
webster_full: SNARE, n. [Sax. snear, a cord.] An instrument for catching animals, particularly birds, by the leg or neck.
2. Anything by which one is entangled and brought into trouble.
3. As a verb, to catch with a snare; to entangle; to bring into unexpected evil.
4. In Scripture, the fear of man bringeth a snare, Prov. 29.
5. Of the devil's trap; as, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil, 1 Tim. 3.
corruption_summary: The fear of man is not usually recognised as sin at all; it passes for tact, prudence, or kindness. Proverbs calls it a snare and sets it against trust in the LORD as the direct alternative.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 29:25 is among the most quietly convicting verses in Scripture because the sin it names is so respectable. Very few men will admit to being afraid of other men; they will say they are being wise, or keeping the peace, or choosing their battles. The verse does not allow the euphemisms. It calls the thing a snare, which means it is a trap and the man in it is caught, and it offers only one alternative — trust in the LORD. Peter denied his Lord to a servant girl, and Aaron made a calf because the people were set on it; both were snared this way.

The principle to recover is the mechanism a snare depends on. It works by being invisible, so a man does not decide to be trapped; he discovers he is. That is why Paul requires an overseer to have a good report from those outside the church — a life already exposed to unsympathetic eyes is much harder to snare. And Psalm 124:7 keeps the hope where Scripture always puts it: the bird did not out-fly the fowler, and the man does not out-think the devil. The snare is broken, and we are escaped.
roots_summary: Hebrew pach is a fowler's snare or net, and moqesh the bait-stick that springs the trap. Greek pagis is a snare, and skandalon the trigger of a trap, hence a stumbling block.

pos: n. (harm deliberately devised; rendering Hebrew amal and awen)
etymology: From the Old French meschief, from mes-, badly, and chief, head or end — a bad outcome, a coming to a bad head. The modern sense of harmless naughtiness is a great weakening; in the Authorized Version mischief is always serious and usually premeditated.
biblical_def: Mischief in the Authorized Version is not childish naughtiness but harm deliberately planned, and the word's force lies in that deliberation. The Psalter describes its conception in the language of pregnancy: “Behold, he travaileth with iniquity, and hath conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood” (Psalm 7:14) — sin gestates, and what is carried is eventually delivered. David locates the planning in the place a man is most alone: “He deviseth mischief upon his bed; he setteth himself in a way that is not good; he abhorreth not evil” (Psalm 36:4). The sleepless hours are where mischief is drafted, which is why Scripture so often speaks of meditating on God's law in the night watches — the mind will work on something. Proverbs includes it in the seven things the LORD hates, naming the organ responsible: “An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief” (Proverbs 6:18). And it pairs the heart with the mouth: “their heart studieth destruction, and their lips talk of mischief” (Proverbs 24:2) — what is studied inwardly comes out in speech, and the talk betrays the study.
webster_summary: Harm deliberately devised — not the modern sense of harmless naughtiness. Scripture describes it conceived like a pregnancy, drafted on a man's bed at night, and betrayed by his speech.
webster_full: MISCHIEF, n. [Old Fr. meschief; mes, bad, and chief, head, end.] Harm; hurt; injury; damage; evil, whether intended or not.
2. Intentional injury; harm or damage done by design.
3. Ill consequence; evil result; as, the mischiefs of intemperance.
4. In Scripture, premeditated wrong; as, he deviseth mischief upon his bed, Psa. 36.
5. Among the things the Lord hates; as, feet that be swift in running to mischief, Prov. 6.
corruption_summary: The word has been trivialised into playfulness — a mischievous child, a mischievous grin — and its biblical weight is gone. In Scripture mischief is premeditated harm, conceived, carried, and delivered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift is semantic softening rather than doctrinal attack, but it has a doctrinal cost. When mischief means mild naughtiness, Proverbs 6:18 sounds like a complaint about boisterous children rather than a listing among the seven things the LORD hates. The Hebrew words behind it — amal, toilsome trouble, and awen, iniquity and vanity — are grave, and the Psalms use them of men plotting a neighbour's ruin.

The principle to recover is Psalm 36:4 and its uncomfortable observation about where sin is planned. A man devises mischief on his bed, in the hours when nobody is watching and nothing external restrains the imagination. Scripture's counter is not merely to stop thinking but to give the mind better work: in his law doth he meditate day and night, and my soul shall be satisfied… when I remember thee upon my bed. Psalm 7:14 supplies the sober conclusion. What is conceived is eventually born, and no one carries a plan indefinitely without delivering it.
roots_summary: Hebrew amal is toilsome trouble or mischief, and awen is iniquity, vanity, and trouble together; ra is evil generally. The Hebrew regularly pairs conception language with these words.
roots_lines: Hebrew amal (H5999) — toil, trouble, mischief; the labour of a man bent on harm.
Hebrew awen (H205) — iniquity, vanity, trouble; the workers of iniquity in the Psalms.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to devise, to reckon, to plot; the verb of premeditation.
Hebrew ra (H7451) — evil, wickedness, calamity; the general word for what is bad.
Greek rhadiourgia (G4468) — mischief, unscrupulousness; Paul's word to Elymas in Acts 13:10.

Of where it is planned: he deviseth mischief upon his bed (Psalm 36:4).
Of what the LORD hates: feet that be swift in running to mischief (Proverbs 6:18).

pos: n. (ceremonial or moral impurity; rendering Hebrew tumah, Greek akatharsia)
etymology: From unclean, Saxon unclaene, with the ending -ness. Hebrew tumah is ritual defilement, a state rather than an act — a man became unclean by contact with death, disease, or discharge, and could not approach the sanctuary until cleansed, whether or not he had sinned.
biblical_def: Uncleanness in Scripture begins as a ceremonial category and becomes a moral one, and the two are connected by design. Under the law a man could be unclean without being guilty — by touching a corpse, by childbirth, by disease — and the point of the system was not hygiene but instruction: God is holy, death and corruption cannot come near him, and access requires cleansing. The stakes are stated bluntly: “Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness; that they die not in their uncleanness, when they defile my tabernacle that is among them” (Leviticus 15:31). The New Testament carries the word over to moral defilement, chiefly sexual. Paul lists it among the sins not even to be named among saints: “fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints” (Ephesians 5:3), and states the alternative in a sentence: “God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness” (1 Thessalonians 4:7). Romans makes uncleanness itself a judgment: “God also gave them up to uncleanness through the lusts of their own hearts” (Romans 1:24) — the giving-up is the penalty, and the sin is its own punishment.
webster_summary: Impurity — ceremonial under the law, moral in the New Testament. The Levitical system taught that corruption cannot approach a holy God; Paul says God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness.
webster_full: UNCLEANNESS, n. [from unclean.] Foulness; dirtiness; filthiness.
2. Want of ritual or ceremonial purity, under the Levitical law.
3. Moral impurity; defilement by sin; especially, lewdness; unchastity.
4. In Scripture, that they die not in their uncleanness, Lev. 15.
5. God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness, 1 Thess. 4.
corruption_summary: Sexual purity is presented as a private preference or an outdated restriction, and the very notion of defilement is treated as shaming. Scripture makes purity a matter of the call of God and locates the defilement in the heart.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern position holds that consensual conduct cannot defile anyone, and that language of uncleanness is itself the harm. Scripture's answer is not primarily about consequences but about calling: God hath not called us unto uncleanness, but unto holiness. The Christian sexual ethic is not a set of restrictions attached to an otherwise neutral life; it follows from what a believer has been called and joined to, which is why Paul argues from the body being the temple of the Holy Ghost rather than from harm.

Romans 1:24 supplies the point most often missed in these debates. Paul does not present uncleanness merely as an offence that will be judged later; he presents God's giving men up to it as itself a judgment now. A society progressively unable to see anything wrong is not escaping the verdict but experiencing it. The principle to recover is that the Levitical system was teaching all along what the gospel then answers: the unclean cannot approach, and the remedy is a cleansing God provides — the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.
roots_summary: Hebrew tumah is ritual uncleanness, from tame, to be defiled; taher is to be clean. Greek akatharsia is impurity, from a- and kathairo, to cleanse — the root of English catharsis.
roots_lines: Hebrew tumah (H2932) — ritual uncleanness, defilement; a state barring approach to the sanctuary.
Hebrew tame (H2930) — to be or become unclean; the verb of Levitical defilement.
Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean, to purify; create in me a clean heart, O God.
Greek akatharsia (G167) — uncleanness, impurity; listed with fornication in Ephesians 5:3.
Greek hagiasmos (G38) — sanctification, holiness; the alternative named in 1 Thessalonians 4:7.
usage: Of the seriousness of ceremonial defilement: that they die not in their uncleanness (Leviticus 15:31).
Of what is not to be named among saints: fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness (Ephesians 5:3).
Of uncleanness as itself a judgment: God also gave them up to uncleanness (Romans 1:24).

pos: n. pl. (acts of harlotry; figuratively, covenant unfaithfulness; rendering Hebrew zenunim)
etymology: From whore, Saxon hore, with the ending -dom denoting condition or state, as in freedom and kingdom. Hebrew zenunim is a plural of intensity from zanah, to commit fornication, and in the prophets it is applied to Israel's idolatry far more often than to literal immorality.
biblical_def: Whoredoms is the prophets' word for idolatry, and the choice of vocabulary is itself the doctrine: because the covenant is a marriage, its breach is adultery rather than mere disobedience. God commands Hosea to enact it: “Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms and children of whoredoms: for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD” (Hosea 1:2) — a prophet's marriage made into a living sermon, so that Israel could see what she looked like. Jeremiah presses the charge over the whole landscape: “Lift up thine eyes unto the high places, and see where thou hast not been lien with… and thou hast polluted the land with thy whoredoms and with thy wickedness” (Jeremiah 3:2). Hosea names the mechanism, which is not appetite but a settled disposition: “the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err, and they have gone a whoring from under their God” (Hosea 4:12). And the word attaches to a name that became a byword when Jehu answered Joram, asking what peace there could be “so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel and her witchcrafts are so many?” (2 Kings 9:22).
webster_summary: Acts of harlotry, and in the prophets the standing figure for idolatry — because the covenant is a marriage, breaking it is adultery. Hosea was commanded to enact the charge in his own household.
webster_full: WHOREDOMS, n. plural of whoredom. [from whore, Sax. hore, with the termination -dom, state or condition.] Lewdness; fornication; practice of unlawful commerce with the other sex.
2. In Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the true God for false gods.
3. Unfaithfulness to a covenant, viewed as marital treachery.
4. As in Hosea; the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the Lord, Hos. 1.
5. The whoredoms of Jezebel and her witchcrafts, 2 Kings 9.
corruption_summary: Idolatry is imagined as a foreign and antique problem, and the marital language of the prophets is thought excessive. Scripture chooses that language deliberately, because the covenant is a marriage and its breach is betrayal rather than mere rule-breaking.
corruption_paragraphs: The instinct to soften this vocabulary misses why God chose it. Had Israel's sin been merely the breaking of rules, the language of trespass would have sufficed; the prophets reach for the language of a betrayed husband because the relationship is a marriage covenant, and the wound is personal. Hosea is the extreme case: God does not only say it, he makes his prophet live it, so that Israel watching Hosea buy back his wife would see what God was doing with her. To flinch from the word is to lose the tenderness underneath it, since the same book says I will betroth thee unto me for ever.

The principle to recover is that idolatry is perennial and domestic. John ends his epistle with little children, keep yourselves from idols, written to Christians, not to pagans; and Paul says covetousness is idolatry. Hosea 4:12 identifies the trouble as a spirit of whoredoms, a settled bent rather than an isolated lapse, which is why the remedy in Scripture is never mere resolution but a new heart. And 2 Kings 9:22 answers the question every compromising generation asks — is it peace? — with the only honest reply: what peace, so long as the whoredoms are so many?
roots_summary: Hebrew zenunim is whoredoms, a plural of intensity from zanah, to play the harlot; taznuth is the same idea. Greek porneia renders it, giving English pornography, and is used of spiritual as well as bodily fornication.
roots_lines: Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit fornication, to go a whoring; used of Israel after other gods.
Hebrew zenunim (H2183) — whoredoms; the intensive plural of Hosea 1:2.
Hebrew taznuth (H8457) — harlotry, whoredom; Ezekiel's term in his indictment of Jerusalem.
Hebrew naaph (H5003) — to commit adultery; the covenant breach stated in marital terms.
Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; used of Babylon's spiritual harlotry in Revelation.
usage: Of the charge enacted in a prophet's household: the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD (Hosea 1:2).
Of a settled disposition rather than a lapse: the spirit of whoredoms hath caused them to err (Hosea 4:12).
Of the impossibility of peace with them: so long as the whoredoms of thy mother Jezebel… are so many (2 Kings 9:22).

pos: n. (penalty inflicted for wrong; rendering Hebrew avon, Greek kolasis)
etymology: From the Latin punio, to punish, from poena, a penalty — the same root as pain and penalty. Hebrew avon means both the iniquity and the punishment of it, so that the Hebrew reader hears the sin and its penalty in one word, and translators must decide which the context intends.
biblical_def: Punishment is penalty justly inflicted, and Scripture treats it as the necessary counterpart of moral law. The first man to use the word is the first murderer: “And Cain said unto the LORD, My punishment is greater than I can bear” (Genesis 4:13) — a sentence that may equally be rendered mine iniquity is greater than can be forgiven, since the Hebrew word carries both, and Cain's complaint is about the weight rather than the justice of it. Lamentations turns the argument on the sufferer: “Wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins?” (Lamentations 3:39) — the mercy is that he is living at all. Hebrews reasons from lesser to greater about those who despise the gospel: “Of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, who hath trodden under foot the Son of God” (Hebrews 10:29), so that greater light received makes rejection graver. And our Lord fixes the duration with a parallel that cannot be broken: “these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal” (Matthew 25:46) — one adjective governs both clauses, and the punishment lasts precisely as long as the life.
webster_summary: Penalty justly inflicted. Hebrew avon means both iniquity and its penalty. Matthew 25:46 sets everlasting punishment in exact parallel with life eternal — one word governing both.
webster_full: PUNISHMENT, n. [from punish; L. punio, from poena, penalty.] Any pain or suffering inflicted on a person for a crime or offense, by the authority to which the offender is subject.
2. The penalty itself, as distinguished from chastisement, which is corrective.
3. In law, the sentence pronounced and executed upon an offender.
4. In Scripture, of Cain; as, my punishment is greater than I can bear, Gen. 4.
5. Of the final state; as, these shall go away into everlasting punishment, Matt. 25.
corruption_summary: Punishment is reduced to deterrence or rehabilitation, so that justice becomes management. Scripture treats penalty as owed to wrong itself, which is precisely what makes substitutionary atonement necessary and coherent.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern penal theory tends to justify punishment only by its results — deterring others, reforming the offender, protecting the public. On that account, punishing a man for whom none of these results obtains is irrational. Scripture holds a retributive view: the wrong itself deserves penalty, quite apart from useful outcomes, which is why the law limits punishment to what fits the crime (eye for eye, and no more) rather than allowing whatever quantity would best deter. Justice is owed, not calculated.

That is not an abstract point, because the doctrine of the atonement stands on it. If punishment is merely deterrence or reform, the cross is unintelligible — nobody is reformed or deterred by an innocent man's death in his place. If penalty is genuinely owed, then it can be borne by a substitute, and the gospel is precisely that Christ bore it. Matthew 25:46 fixes the alternative for those who refuse him, and the grammar allows no softening: the same word describes the punishment and the life, so a punishment that ends requires a life that ends with it.
roots_summary: Hebrew avon is iniquity and also its penalty; paqad is to visit, to call to account. Greek kolasis is punishment or correction, and timoria is retributive penalty, the word in Hebrews 10:29.
roots_lines: Hebrew avon (H5771) — iniquity, and the punishment of iniquity; Cain's word in Genesis 4:13.
Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, to number, to call to account; visiting the iniquity of the fathers.
Hebrew musar (H4148) — chastening, correction, discipline; distinguished from penal punishment.
Greek kolasis (G2851) — punishment; the word in everlasting punishment, Matthew 25:46.
Greek timoria (G5098) — retribution, penalty; of how much sorer punishment, Hebrews 10:29.
usage: Of the first murderer's complaint: my punishment is greater than I can bear (Genesis 4:13).
Of the mercy of being alive at all: wherefore doth a living man complain, a man for the punishment of his sins? (Lamentations 3:39).
Of the final state in exact parallel with eternal life: these shall go away into everlasting punishment (Matthew 25:46).

pos: n. (disorder, shame; rendering Hebrew bosheth and tohu, Greek akatastasia)
etymology: From the Latin confusio, from confundo, to pour together. Hebrew bosheth is shame, and tohu is formlessness — the word describing the earth before the third day — so biblical confusion is both disorder and the disgrace attending it.
biblical_def: Confusion in Scripture is disorder, and disorder is presented as contrary to God's nature rather than merely inconvenient. Its origin as a proper name is Babel: “Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth” (Genesis 11:9) — a judgment on a united humanity building a tower to make itself a name, and the confusion of tongues is the scattering of that project. Paul makes the theological principle explicit and applies it to worship: “God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1 Corinthians 14:33). The argument is from the divine character to the shape of a service, which is why order in the assembly is a matter of obedience and not preference. James names the source of confusion in a congregation with uncomfortable precision: “where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (James 3:16) — not doctrinal error in that instance but envy, the sin nobody confesses. The word also carries the older sense of shame, in which the Psalmist prays to be spared: “In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust: let me never be put to confusion” (Psalm 71:1).
webster_summary: Disorder, and also shame. Babel is confusion as judgment; Paul argues from God's character that he is not the author of confusion but of peace; James traces it in a church to envy and strife.
webster_full: CONFUSION, n. [L. confusio, from confundo, to pour together.] In a general sense, a mixture of several things promiscuously; hence, disorder; irregularity.
2. Tumult; want of order in society; as, a city in confusion.
3. Abashment; shame; as, he was put to confusion before them all.
4. Astonishment; agitation; distraction of mind.
5. In Scripture, God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, 1 Cor. 14; the name of it called Babel, Gen. 11.
corruption_summary: Disorder in worship is defended as spiritual liberty, and disorder in a church is blamed on personalities or structures. Paul grounds order in the character of God, and James traces confusion to envy and strife.
corruption_paragraphs: The claim that structured worship quenches the Spirit runs directly into 1 Corinthians 14, the chapter most concerned with the extraordinary gifts, which regulates them and concludes that all things be done decently and in order. Paul's reason is not pragmatic. He says God is not the author of confusion but of peace, so a disorderly assembly misrepresents the God it gathers to worship. The regulative principle follows from this: worship is ordered by what God has commanded, because the God who commands is himself a God of peace.

James 3:16 supplies the harder diagnosis, and it is one congregations resist. When a church falls into confusion, the causes offered are usually structural or personal — poor communication, difficult members, unclear leadership. James names envying and strife, and adds every evil work, meaning confusion is not only a symptom but a doorway. The principle to recover is that the remedy runs through repentance rather than reorganisation, and the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated.
roots_summary: Hebrew bosheth is shame, tohu is formlessness or vanity, and balal is to mingle or confound — the verb behind the name Babel. Greek akatastasia is instability, tumult, or confusion.
roots_lines: Hebrew balal (H1101) — to mingle, to confound; the verb from which Babel is named.
Hebrew bosheth (H1322) — shame, confusion of face; the older English sense of the word.
Hebrew tohu (H8414) — formlessness, waste, vanity; the earth was without form, Genesis 1:2.
Greek akatastasia (G181) — instability, disorder, tumult; the word in 1 Corinthians 14:33.
Greek eirene (G1515) — peace; what God is the author of instead of confusion.
usage: Of the judgment at Babel: because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth (Genesis 11:9).
Of God's character governing worship: God is not the author of confusion, but of peace (1 Corinthians 14:33).
Of its source in a congregation: where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work (James 3:16).
